questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: Defining a Disorder by Distress and Impairment Rather Than by Symptoms Alone
questions.learningObjective: state what a definition of disorder has to add to a symptom list
questions.stem: A person has a symptom that appears in one published diagnostic scheme, but the symptom is mild, causes no impairment, and the person does not want it changed. Under the standard definition, is a disorder present?

options.text: Yes, because the symptom appears in a published scheme, and appearing in a scheme is what makes a disorder
options.misconception: treats membership of a symptom list as sufficient, dropping the distress and impairment conditions entirely

options.text: No, because a disorder requires distress or impairment as well as symptoms, and neither of the first two is present here
No, because the person must want the symptom changed, and a lack of that wish rules out a disorder by definition
options.misconception: makes the patient's own wish the deciding criterion, when the standard definition requires distress or impairment rather than a stated wish

options.text: It cannot be decided, because no published definition of disorder includes a criterion about severity
options.misconception: asserts that severity is absent from every definition, when it is a standard part of them

questions.explanation: The vignette is built to satisfy one condition and fail two others, and the answer turns on noticing which. The symptom is real and appears in a scheme, so the first condition holds. It is mild, so severity is not established. It causes no impairment, and the person reports no distress. Standard definitions require symptoms plus distress or impairment plus something of severity, so all three conditions must hold and two of them do not. That is the correct reading. The option that admits the diagnosis on symptom membership alone drops two conditions and is the single most common error in thinking about diagnosis. The option making the patient's stated wish decisive confuses the definition with a treatment decision; a person can find a symptom troubling without asking for its removal, and can want a symptom removed without it being a disorder. The final option denies that severity appears in definitions when it is standard in them.
questions.hint: Count the conditions the vignette satisfies and the conditions it fails, and ask whether all of them are needed.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: Why Absent Harm Is Not the Criterion
questions.learningObjective: explain why harmfulness is not sufficient for a disorder and is not necessary either
questions.stem: A widely used definition says a disorder is a clinically significant dysfunction in an individual's behavioural, biological or cognitive system, associated with present distress or disability. Which observation is hardest for that definition to handle?

options.text: That some people distress greatly over a condition no clinician regards as disordered
options.misconception: takes this to be a counterexample, when the definition's requirement of a dysfunction is what excludes these cases

options.text: That a condition can be mild in one person and severe in another while being the same condition
options.misconception: supplies a variation in degree, which the definition handles by requiring significance rather than a fixed severity

options.text: That some conditions cause substantial harm without producing distress or disability in the person who has them
That two clinicians can disagree about whether a dysfunction is present in the same person
options.misconception: supplies disagreement between raters, which is a measurement problem the definition does not purport to solve

questions.explanation: The definition names distress or disability as a necessary part, and a condition producing no distress or disability in the person who has it sits awkwardly against that, because the condition is still a dysfunction of a system. This is the well-known difficulty the definition is usually said to have, and identifying it is the point of the item. It is the hard observation rather than a refutation, since the definition can be defended by arguing the dysfunction is then not clinically significant in the required sense, or by revising it. The other options are not counterexamples at all. Distress over something not disordered is excluded by the dysfunction clause rather than threatened by it. Variation in degree is anticipated by the significance requirement. Disagreement between raters is a reliability question that no definition of disorder can settle by definition, and treating it as a counterexample confuses two different problems.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the definition has no room for a condition that harms without distressing its owner.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: Deviation From the Statistical Norm and What That Cannot Say
questions.learningObjective: evaluate an argument from statistical rarity to disorder
questions.stem: Someone argues that a trait should count as a disorder if fewer than 1 in 1,000 people have it, because that makes it rare. What is wrong with the argument?

options.text: That the 1 in 1,000 figure cannot be measured accurately, since any prevalence estimate carries sampling error
options.misconception: treats a measurement objection as the substantive one, when the argument would fail even with a perfectly measured prevalence

options.text: That rare conditions are usually missed because clinicians expect to see them often
options.misconception: invents a clinical inattention effect that the argument never appeals to

options.text: That the threshold of 1 in 1,000 is far too strict, since most disorders are rarer than that
options.misconception: objects to the particular cut-off rather than to the use of rarity itself, so it would leave the argument standing with a different number

options.text: That rarity is a property of many harmless and even adaptive traits, so it does not identify anything clinically significant

questions.explanation: The argument commits a straightforward error: it takes a necessary-looking property and treats it as sufficient. Rarity is not sufficient, because plenty of rare traits are harmless and some are useful, and none of them becomes a disorder by being uncommon. This is why every standard definition adds distress, impairment and clinical significance rather than relying on frequency, and it is what the correct option states. The option about measurement accuracy attacks a different thing, and it is worth separating the two carefully: even a prevalence known with no error at all would not make the argument work, because the argument is about what follows from rarity rather than about how well rarity is known. The option about clinicians missing rare conditions introduces a claim about practice that the argument does not use. The final option is the one to watch for, since it objects only to the number and leaves the reasoning intact, so accepting it would mean accepting the argument with 1 in 10,000 instead.
questions.hint: Ask whether being rare is enough to make anything disordered, and what that implies about the argument's logic.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: What Each Part of a Multi-Axis Diagnosis Is For
questions.learningObjective: identify the function each axis of a multi-axis diagnosis serves
questions.stem: A diagnostic system that records several things about each case rather than one label is described. Which statements about the purposes those parts serve are supported? Select the two supported statements.

options.text: Recording the current clinically significant symptoms separates what is present now from what has been present in the past
Recording the axis on which the condition is mainly psychological or mainly biological settles the underlying cause, since the two cannot both be implicated
options.misconception: treats the axis as an etiological finding, when it is an organising convention rather than a causal claim

options.text: Recording severity and duration separately captures information a single label cannot, because two cases with the same label can differ on both
options.misconception: claims severity and duration carry no separate information, although they vary independently within a single category

options.text: Recording the level of functioning separately captures something a symptom count cannot, since a person can have many symptoms and still function well
options.misconception: asserts functioning adds nothing to a symptom count, which it plainly does when the two dissociate

questions.explanation: The two supported statements are the first and the third. Keeping present symptoms separate from the history is what allows a system to distinguish a current episode from a past one, and without that separation a chronic label would absorb acute states it does not describe. Recording severity and duration separately captures variation that a single label necessarily flattens, since two people with the same diagnosis can differ substantially on both dimensions, and that difference matters for what is done next. The unsupported statements are the second and the fourth. The psychological-versus-biological axis is an organising convention that records which presentation is being emphasised; it is not a finding about aetiology, and nothing in a multi-axis system claims the causes are exclusive. The functioning axis exists precisely because functioning dissociates from symptom count, and a system that dropped it would lose exactly the information that distinguishes a person who is unwell but coping from one who is not.
questions.hint: Ask which parts of the record describe something happening now, which describe variation inside one label, and which claim to settle a cause.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: A Threshold Placed on a Continuous Distribution
questions.learningObjective: explain what a cut point on a continuum does and does not represent
questions.stem: A score is normally distributed in the general population. A cut point is placed so that the top 10 percent of the distribution count as cases. Which statement about that choice is correct?

options.text: The 10 percent is the prevalence of the disorder, since everyone above the cut has the disorder by construction
options.misconception: confuses the share the definition admits with the share that has the condition, which is the base-rate problem

options.text: The 10 percent is a property of where the cut was placed, not a finding about how many disordered people there are
The 10 percent shows the disorder is common, since one person in ten meeting a definition is by any standard a high rate
options.misconception: reports the figure the definition produced as though it were a fact about the disorder

options.text: The 10 percent means the cut was placed correctly, since a well-chosen threshold should select the true number of cases
options.misconception: supposes a threshold can be chosen to match a number it is supposed to determine

questions.explanation: This item separates two quantities that are constantly run together. The cut point defines who counts, so the share above it is a consequence of where the cut was put and would be 5 percent or 20 percent for a different cut, chosen by the same reasoning. How many people actually have the condition is a separate quantity, discovered by finding out what proportion of the flagged group actually has it, and it depends on the base rate and on how well the score separates cases. That is the correct reading, and it is the base-rate problem in its cleanest form. The option calling the 10 percent the prevalence makes the definition do the measuring. The option calling it evidence of a common disorder has the same error with a conclusion attached. The option claiming a well-chosen cut selects the true number reverses the direction of dependence, since a threshold cannot be chosen to match a number it is supposed to be measuring.
questions.hint: Ask whether the 10 percent was discovered by measuring people or produced by the definition.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: Two Clinicians Judging Sixty Cases
questions.learningObjective: compute an agreement statistic that adjusts for chance agreement
questions.stem: Two clinicians each classify 60 cases into three categories. The numbers in which they agree, counted on the diagonal of the table, are 22, 20 and 0, so 42 of the 60 agree. If they had been assigning categories independently, the chance agreement would have been 0.42. Using the chance-adjusted form, what is the value?
questions.explanation: The chance-adjusted statistic here is the kappa form, which removes the agreement two raters would produce by chance alone. Observed agreement is 42 over 60, which is 0.70. Chance agreement is given as 0.42. The correction subtracts the chance term and divides by what is left of the possible range, giving (0.70 minus 0.42) divided by (1 minus 0.42), which is 0.28 over 0.58, and that is 0.4828, so about 0.48. The reason this matters is visible in the two numbers side by side. Raw agreement of 0.70 looks respectable, and by itself it is uninterpretable, because raters agree 42 percent of the time purely because the categories are unevenly distributed, with 28 cases in each of the first two categories and only 4 in the third. Once that free agreement is removed, what is left is a little under chance-corrected mid-range, which says the two clinicians' judgements were related but far from interchangeable. Reporting only the 0.70 would have been misleading, and the discrepancy between the two figures is the whole reason the adjusted form exists.
questions.hint: Subtract the chance agreement from the observed agreement, then divide by what remains of the possible range.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: Agreement Between Raters Is Not Validity
questions.learningObjective: distinguish reliability of a judgement from validity of what is judged
questions.stem: Two clinicians agree on the diagnosis for 90 percent of cases, but an independent criterion shows that 40 percent of those diagnoses are wrong. Which statement about this situation is correct?

options.text: The measure is highly valid and poorly reliable, since consistency with a criterion is the definition of validity
options.misconception: confuses agreement between raters with agreement with a criterion, which are different things entirely

options.text: Neither figure is interpretable, since reliability and validity cannot be assessed on the same data
options.misconception: insulates the finding from interpretation by declaring both quantities unmeasurable together

options.text: The measure is unreliable, since a clinician making 40 percent errors cannot be consistent with anyone
options.misconception: treats a high error rate against a criterion as evidence of inconsistency, when consistency was measured directly

options.text: The measure is highly reliable and of doubtful validity, since the raters are consistent with each other and wrong together

questions.explanation: Two separate quantities are being reported and they can move independently. Reliability is whether the instrument gives the same answer when applied twice or by two raters, and 90 percent agreement says it does. Validity is whether the answer is correct against something outside the instrument, and 40 percent error against the criterion says it is not, at least in part. A measure can be perfectly consistent and consistently wrong, which is exactly what the description describes. That is the correct reading, and the situation is common, because a shared misreading of a criterion is what systematic error looks like. The option reversing the two quantities misdefines validity as agreement among raters. The option declaring both uninterpretable mistakes an awkward finding for an impossibility. The option treating a criterion error rate as inconsistency confuses the two quantities once more, this time in the opposite direction.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two reported numbers comes from comparing the instrument with itself, and which from comparing it with something outside.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: A Clinic Sample and Why Its Rates Do Not Transfer
questions.learningObjective: explain why a rate measured in a clinic sample does not estimate community prevalence
questions.stem: A specialist clinic sees 1,000 patients in a year and records 400 who meet criteria for a disorder. A community survey in the same region draws 200 people at random and finds 20 who meet the same criteria. Which statement about these figures is correct?

options.text: The two rates are 40 percent and 10 percent, and the clinic figure is four times the community figure because the clinic sample is not a random sample of the region
The two rates are 40 percent and 10 percent, and the difference shows the disorder is four times more common in people who seek care
options.misconception: states the selection effect backwards, since care-seeking is what was selected for and not an outcome the disorder produced

options.text: The counts of 400 and 20 differ by a factor of 20, so the disorder is twenty times more common in clinic patients
options.misconception: compares raw counts of differently sized samples, which is the denominator error

options.text: The community rate is the biased figure, since random sampling is guaranteed to overstate the prevalence of a hidden condition
options.misconception: asserts random sampling must bias a prevalence estimate upward, which is not a property of random sampling

questions.explanation: The first step is two divisions with two different denominators. Four hundred over one thousand is 0.40, and 20 over 200 is 0.10, so the clinic rate is four times the community rate, not twenty times, because comparing 400 with 20 compares counts drawn from samples that differ in size by a factor of five. What the fourfold difference reflects is the sampling. Clinic patients are people who sought care, and a clinic sample is therefore enriched for people whose symptoms are severe, novel, or otherwise brought them to that door, so it is not a random sample of the region and its rate cannot be read as the population rate. That is what the correct option says. The option reading the difference as a fact about who seeks care states the selection effect in the wrong direction, since care-seeking is what was selected for rather than an outcome the disorder produced. The option comparing raw counts is the denominator error stated explicitly. The option asserting that random sampling must overstate a hidden condition mistakes a possible bias for a necessary one.
questions.hint: Divide each count by its own sample size, then ask what makes the two samples different in kind rather than in size.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: A Cut Point Set on a Well-Being Scale
questions.learningObjective: compute the share of flagged cases that are real from a base rate and test rates
questions.stem: In a group of 1,000 people the condition is present for 8 percent, so 80 people have it and 920 do not. A questionnaire is set so that anyone scoring in the top 10 percent is flagged, and among the 80 who have the condition 80 percent are flagged, while among the 920 who do not, 10 percent are flagged. First work out how many people are flagged, then what share of the flagged are real.

options.text: 156 people are flagged, and about 41 percent of them are real, since the false positives are added to the 64 found
options.misconception: adds 92 false positives on top of a positive total that already contained them, double counting the wrongly flagged group

options.text: 100 people are flagged, and about 41 percent of them are real, since 80 percent of 80 is 64 against 10 percent of 920 being 92
100 people are flagged, and about 80 percent of them are real, since that is the proportion of true cases that were caught
options.misconception: reports the sensitivity as though it were the share of positives that are real, which uses the wrong denominator

options.text: 156 people are flagged, and about 64 percent of them are real, since 64 of 100 real cases is that share
options.misconception: combines a doubled positive total with a sensitivity figure, so both the count and the share are wrong

questions.explanation: The two steps have to be done in that order, and the base rate does all the work in the first. Eighty of the thousand have the condition and 920 do not, so the flagging rate cannot be applied to a thousand people as though it were uniform. Among the 80 who have it, 80 percent are flagged, which is 64. Among the 920 who do not, 10 percent are flagged, which is 92. The positives are therefore 64 plus 92, which is 156, and the share of them that are real is 64 over 156, which is 41.0 percent. The correct option states the count as 100, which is the number the questionnaire's own threshold produces, and its share as 41 percent, and the reasoning in the option is the point. The option that adds the false positives to an already-inclusive total double counts them. The option reporting 80 percent has taken the sensitivity and used it as though it were the share of positives that are real; the two are different quantities with different denominators, and the whole point of the item is that the second is much lower than the first. The final option combines both errors.
questions.hint: Apply each flagging rate to the group it belongs to, add the two flag counts, and divide the real ones by the total.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: Two Stages of Screening With Two Different Thresholds
questions.learningObjective: compute the effect of adding a second screening stage on the share of positives that are real
questions.stem: A population of 10,000 is screened in two stages for a condition affecting 1 percent. Stage 1 catches 90 percent of those with it and wrongly flags 20 percent of those without it. Everyone flagged by stage 1 is then given stage 2, which catches 95 percent of the remaining true cases among those it sees and wrongly flags 10 percent of the others it sees. First work out how many are flagged by stage 1, then what share of the flagged remain after stage 2.

options.text: 2,070 are flagged by stage 1 and about 4 percent of the final positives are real, since that is the share before stage 2 is applied
options.misconception: reports the share before the second stage rather than after, so the second stage does no work in the calculation

options.text: 2,970 are flagged by stage 1, since 20 percent of the 9,900 without the condition should be added to the 100 with it
options.misconception: adds the wrongly flagged to a count of the whole unaffected group instead of taking 20 percent of it

options.text: 2,070 are flagged by stage 1 and about 30 percent of the final positives are real, since 198 of the wrongly flagged are removed by stage 2
2,070 are flagged by stage 1 and about 86 percent of the final positives are real, since stage 2 catches 95 percent of the true cases
options.misconception: reports stage 2's sensitivity as the share of positives that are real, which again swaps the denominators

questions.explanation: Of the ten thousand people, a hundred have the condition and 9,900 do not. Stage 1 catches 90 percent of the hundred, which is 90, and wrongly flags 20 percent of the 9,900, which is 1,980. So 2,070 are flagged and move to stage 2, and the share of them that are real at that point is 90 over 2,070, which is 4.3 percent. Stage 2 now sees only those 2,070, of whom 90 are real and 1,980 are not. It keeps 95 percent of the real ones, about 86, and removes 90 percent of the false ones, leaving 198. The final positives are about 86 plus 198, which is 284, and the share that are real is 86 over 284, about 30 percent. That is the correct answer, and the gain from 4.3 percent to 30 percent comes entirely from the second stage being much better at rejecting false positives. The option reporting the pre-second-stage share makes the second stage irrelevant. The option with 2,970 has taken 20 percent of the whole unaffected group and then added the hundred, which is a different quantity. The last option repeats the denominator error from the previous item.
questions.hint: Work out who reaches stage 2 before working out what stage 2 does, since its rates apply to that group only.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: Comorbidity in a Table of Two Diagnoses and an Outcome
questions.learningObjective: read an association between two diagnoses in a contingency table
questions.stem: In a follow-up of 400 people, those with both a mood diagnosis and a substance-use diagnosis number 120, those with only the mood diagnosis 80, those with only the substance-use diagnosis 40, and those with neither 160. Which statements about this table are correct? Select the two that are.

options.text: The odds of the outcome are six times higher among those with both diagnoses than among those with neither
The table shows that one diagnosis causes the other, since the co-occurrence rate is high enough to establish direction
options.misconception: reads a co-occurrence rate as establishing a causal direction, which no observational table can do

options.text: Eighty of the 200 people with the mood diagnosis also carry the substance-use diagnosis, so the two are far from independent
The table shows that 30 percent of people with the mood diagnosis carry the substance-use diagnosis, since 120 is 30 percent of 400
options.misconception: divides a subgroup count by the whole cohort rather than by the subgroup it belongs to

questions.explanation: The two supported statements are the first and the third. The odds ratio is the cross-product of the 120 and the 160 divided by the cross-product of the 80 and the 40, which is 6, so the odds of the outcome are six times higher with both diagnoses than with neither, and the confidence interval on that figure excludes 1. The second supported statement is a within-group rate: 200 people carry the mood diagnosis, of whom 80 also carry the substance-use one, and 80 over 200 is 40 percent, which is far above what independence would give, so the two are associated in this sample. The unsupported statements are the second and the fourth. The table cannot establish that one diagnosis causes the other, because the cases were not assigned and the shared causes are unmeasured; co-occurrence is compatible with one causing the other, with both following a third thing, and with both being selected into follow-up. The final option divides 120 by 400, using the whole cohort as the denominator for a rate that concerns only the mood subgroup, which is exactly the denominator error the earlier items in this unit are built to make visible.
questions.hint: For the odds ratio cross-multiply the table; for the co-occurrence rate divide by the size of the relevant subgroup rather than by the whole cohort.

questions.topic: Disorders: The Debate Over Categories Against Dimensions
questions.learningObjective: state the disagreement between a categorical and a dimensional account
questions.stem: One account holds that a disorder is a category a person either has or does not have. A second holds that relevant characteristics lie on dimensions and that a disorder is a region of those dimensions rather than a separate kind of entity. Which consideration most favours the dimensional account?

options.text: That cases near a boundary are common and are classified differently by different systems, which a category boundary handles badly
That categories are administratively convenient, since clinicians must record something that fits a form
options.misconception: gives an argument for the categorical account while being asked for an argument against it

options.text: That dimensional scores require sophisticated measurement equipment, so the categorical account is more practical in ordinary clinics
options.misconception: grounds a dimensional argument in equipment, which is a practical objection rather than a substantive one

options.text: That most people can be assigned to a category without difficulty, which shows the categories are doing useful work
options.misconception: cites the categorical account's strength as though it were the dimensional account's

questions.explanation: The strongest substantive argument for a dimensional account is the boundary problem. If most people sit near the edge of a category rather than in its middle, then where the line is drawn changes who counts, two competent systems can classify the same person differently, and the resulting labels carry less information than the underlying scores. That is what the correct option states. It is worth being clear that this is an argument about description and it is not by itself an argument about causes, since a dimensional score and a category label can both be useful summaries. The other options each fail in the same way. Two of them supply reasons for the categorical account, which is the opposite of what the question asks, and one of those is close enough to a real argument to be worth naming as such. The third substitutes a practical objection about equipment for a substantive one, and the dimensional account does not in fact require expensive measurement to be usable.

questions.topic: Disorders: A General Factor Underlying Many Conditions
questions.learningObjective: evaluate what a general psychopathology factor would and would not explain
questions.stem: Some findings are consistent with a single general factor on which all forms of psychopathology load to some degree, in the way that many cognitive tasks load on a general intelligence factor. Which claim would the existence of such a factor license?

options.text: That the specific diagnostic categories can be discarded, since a single factor would account for every symptom within them
options.misconception: treats a shared component as a complete account, which is the claim the data do not support

options.text: That a shared component contributes to many conditions, which would not identify that component or make the specific categories unnecessary
That the cause of the general factor is known, since a factor recovered from data must correspond to a biological process
options.misconception: confuses a factor extracted from data with a mechanism that produced it

options.text: That conditions which load on the factor are medically the same illness expressed in different ways

The option naming a cause confuses a factor extracted from a correlation matrix with a process that produced it, which is a general and much-missed error. questions.topic: Disorders: Why a Different Arrangement of the Categories Was Proposed
questions.learningObjective: state the methodological criticism that motivated a hierarchical revision
questions.stem: A research framework reorganised the diagnostic categories in nested hierarchies, with spectra of symptoms within broader dimensions, rather than keeping the categories as separate lists. Which criticism of the original arrangement does that revision answer most directly?

options.text: That the original categories were too few to be useful, since more diagnoses would capture more of the variation
options.misconception: mistakes a revision of the organising principle for an increase in the number of labels

options.text: That the original categories were based on too few studies, since the evidence base was assembled too quickly
options.misconception: raises the quantity of the evidence base rather than its structure, which the revision does not address

options.text: That the original categories overlapped in ways that made a single diagnosis arbitrary for many real cases
That the original categories were derived from clinical intuition rather than from any data at all
options.misconception: overstates the criticism to a claim that the original scheme used no data, which is not what the overlap argument says

Where categories share symptoms, a person who meets criteria for several could be assigned to any of them, and two clinicians applying the same list could reasonably choose differently, so the label a person receives depends partly on which clinician they saw. Nesting the categories inside dimensions was intended to reduce that arbitrariness by making clear that a single person can carry graded quantities of several characteristics rather than falling into one box. That is what the correct option identifies. The option about needing more labels misdescribes the revision, which reorganised the existing material rather than adding to it. The option about too few studies is a different objection about evidence quantity and is not addressed by a change in structure. The final option escalates the overlap argument into a claim that no data were involved, which is a much stronger and inaccurate statement.
questions.hint: Ask what a person meeting criteria for several categories should be labelled, and what that ambiguity does to the label's meaning.

questions.topic: Disorders: Disproportionate Fear and the Preparation It Buys
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the functional account of a fear whose object does not match its cause
questions.stem: A fear of a specific harmless object is said to be adaptive because a stimulus similar to it once signalled danger, so the response was prepared by evolution. Which criticism does this account invite?

options.text: That the fear must be learned before it can be useful, since a prepared response is by definition acquired
options.misconception: denies that prepared responses can be innate, which is the sense the account relies on

options.text: That most fears are not specific to objects, since preparation requires a general readiness rather than a particular stimulus
options.misconception: generalises from one kind of fear to all fears, which the account is not making

options.text: That the account implies the fear is deliberate, since a function served by the fear must be intended by the person
options.misconception: imports intention into a functional explanation, which works without any notion of intent

options.text: That a prepared response implies nothing about whether a response that is now costly is still worth making, since the environment has changed

questions.explanation: The functional account explains why a response exists by pointing at what it once did, and that kind of explanation is genuinely informative about origins. What it cannot do on its own is justify the response now, because the explanation is about a past environment and no argument connects that past to whether the response still pays. In a setting where the feared object is harmless and the fear is costly, the origin story is compatible with the fear being a liability, and that is the criticism the correct option makes. The other options each misdescribe the account. Prepared responses in this sense are precisely those not requiring learning, so denying it is to deny the notion. The claim about most fears being general replaces an argument about a particular kind of fear with a statement about all of them. And functional explanations are explicitly indifferent to intention, since they explain a response by its consequences rather than by any purpose the person had.

A fear of a single specific object, since the defining feature of a diagnosis is a fear attached to one identifiable situation
options.misconception: applies the defining feature of a specific phobia to a case with no object at all

options.text: An episode lasting less than a day, since the duration requirement is not met by a complaint of six months
options.misconception: misreads a six-month complaint as a sub-daily episode

options.text: A condition that cannot be diagnosed because the worries are realistic, since only implausible beliefs count as disordered thinking
options.misconception: treats realistic content as disqualifying, when the criteria concern control, duration and impairment rather than the content's realism

questions.learningObjective: explain the interpretation that maintains a panic episode

options.misconception: drops the interpretation out of the loop, leaving sensations to speak for themselves

options.text: A bodily signal is read as evidence of danger, and the reading is acted on in ways that produce further bodily changes
The person is imagining the sensations, since a bodily change that is not dangerous cannot be felt as strongly
options.misconception: supposes the sensations are imagined, which is not what a bodily signal claim requires

options.misconception: makes the interpretation a deliberate act, which no account of this episode requires

The option calling the sensations imagined concedes nothing and explains nothing, since the sensations are not disputed in the account being described. options.misconception: treats a large discrepancy in kind as a discrepancy in detail, which reverses the size of the problem

options.misconception: presumes the observers missed what the speaker noticed, without any basis for preferring their silence to their account

The person is over-reacting to a single instance, since a small sample of one meeting is too little to support any conclusion
options.misconception: objects to the sample size of the meeting rather than to the direction of the prediction

questions.stem: Three statements about repetitive thoughts and behaviours in this condition are offered. Two are supported and one is not. Select the two supported statements.

options.text: An obsession is a recurrent thought that is unwanted and experienced as ego-dystonic, so the person recognises it as not reflecting their own view
A compulsion is a behaviour carried out to reduce anxiety, and the behaviour is recognised by the person as unreasonable
Both are aimed at preventing a feared event from happening, which is what makes them compulsion-like rather than ordinary habit
options.misconception: merges the two into a single function, when they differ in being a thought versus a behaviour and in being wanted versus unwanted

options.text: Neither needs to be related to an obsession, since the two are recognised as independent and may occur separately
options.misconception: denies the relationship the pair is defined by

The distinguishing mark of the behaviour is that it is carried out in order to reduce anxiety and is recognised by the person as unreasonable, which is what separates it from a habit that serves a purpose and is not regarded as pointless. The unsupported statements are the third and the fourth. The third collapses the two into one function and loses everything the diagnosis distinguishes, since one is a thought and one is a behaviour, and one is unwanted while the other is performed. The other options each substitute a non-clinical motive or an invalid inference. Administrative convenience has no place in a clinical inclusion criterion. The dating difficulty is not solved by counting duration from a point that still has to be identified. questions.topic: Disorders: A Threshold of Four Features Across Thirty Observed Days
questions.learningObjective: compute an episode-length share and read it against a criterion
questions.stem: A clinician observes a person over 30 consecutive days and counts, on each day, how many of a set of features are present. On 18 days the count is at or above four, and on the remaining 12 days it is below four. The diagnosis requires the count on at least a third of the days of an episode. As a fraction of the observed days, how many days met the requirement?
questions.explanation: Eighteen days out of thirty is 0.60, and that is the share the question asks for. The comparison with the one-third requirement is a separate step and it holds: one third is 0.333 and 0.60 is well above it, so the observed period meets the requirement as it stands. The arithmetic itself is not the interesting part of this item and the reason to compute it rather than estimate is that the two quantities a reader is likely to compare are easy to confuse. The count of days, 18, is not the share; the share is not the proportion of the features on each day; and the number four is a criterion rather than a measurement. What the episode-length clause is doing in the diagnosis is worth stating, because it is the same clause that separates a disorder from the ordinary fluctuations in mood, energy and motivation that everyone shows. A short run of elevated days is common and mostly resolves; a run sustained over a substantial part of a period is what the requirement is designed to capture. It is also worth being clear that the requirement was set by convention rather than derived, so it is a defensible line rather than a natural break in the data.
questions.hint: Divide the number of days that met the count by the total number of days observed.

questions.topic: Disorders: A First Episode and What Its Outcome Does Not Tell You
questions.learningObjective: explain why the outcome of a first episode does not settle later course
questions.stem: A person is hospitalised after a first episode of losing touch with reality, and recovers over two weeks. Which statement about what this predicts is correct?

options.text: That a good immediate outcome predicts a good long-term course, since recurrence is rare after a single episode
options.misconception: asserts a prospective relation from the one thing that was observed, which is an outcome rather than a course

options.text: That a good immediate outcome identifies the cause, since a condition that remits quickly cannot be biological in origin
options.misconception: infers a mechanism from the time course of recovery

options.text: That a good immediate outcome leaves later course unsettled here, because one person's recovery is one observation and the design supports no prospective claim
That a good immediate outcome rules out a genetic contribution, since an inherited condition would be expected to persist
options.misconception: treats remitting and inherited as incompatible, which confuses course with aetiology

Later course is a different thing, observed over years. A single case of a first quantity is not evidence about the relation between the two, and that is the limit the correct option names, without pretending to a figure the vignette does not supply. Whether that relation is weak, moderate or strong is an empirical question about a sample of first episodes, and it is not answerable from one episode; reports that a first episode's outcome does or does not predict the course are claims about samples, and they should be quoted with their own limitations attached. The option that predicts a good course asserts a relation the vignette cannot establish, and recurrence after a single episode is not rare. The option identifying the cause from the speed of recovery commits the commonest error in this area: a time course is a description and carries no information about mechanism, so a condition that remits quickly may be biological, psychological, or both. The final option treats a slow variable as though it were incompatible with a fast one, which is a confusion between the trajectory of symptoms and the contribution of any inherited factor.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders: What Has to Be Excluded Before a First-Episode Diagnosis
questions.learningObjective: order the considerations bearing on a first-episode diagnosis
questions.stem: Put these five steps in the order they belong in when a person is admitted after a first episode of losing touch with reality.

options.text: Establish that there is currently no substance or medication accounting for the episode
Establish that the episode is not a direct consequence of a general medical condition
Characterise the symptoms present now, including their content and their duration
Establish that the person has not had a previous episode that went unrecognised
Assign the diagnosis, and record the information needed for the differential to be reconsidered if the course changes

questions.explanation: The keyed order is A, B, C, D, E. The reasoning is that exclusions and characterisations are gathered before a label is attached, and that a label at a first episode has to be provisional because the differential is wide and the diagnosis may need revision. A and B come first because both are conditions under which the presentation is not the condition being diagnosed, and both can be established without knowing what the diagnosis will be; getting them wrong means a diagnosis that describes the wrong thing. Characterising the present symptoms follows, since the symptom content and duration determine which criteria are met and what else needs to be asked about. Establishing that there was no earlier unrecognised episode comes next, because that is what makes this a first episode and it changes what the episode means, though not what it is. Only then is the diagnosis assigned, and the last option is the one most often left off: recording what has to be watched in order to revise the diagnosis is what makes a first-episode diagnosis honest rather than definitive.
questions.hint: Exclusions and characterisations are gathered before a label, and a first-episode label has to come with a plan for revising it.

questions.topic: Disorders: The Neurotransmitter Account and the Evidence Under It
questions.learningObjective: state what a neurotransmitter account explains and the objections it meets
questions.stem: An account holds that a condition involving loss of contact with reality arises from altered signalling of a particular neurotransmitter, and that drugs acting on that system alter symptoms. Which objection is most telling?

options.text: That drugs which alter the signalling relieve symptoms without producing the condition, so the system may be downstream of something rather than upstream
That the account is too simple to be useful, since a single system cannot account for a condition with many presentations
options.misconception: objects to explanatory simplicity, which is not in itself a defect in an account

options.text: That the account was formulated before the drugs were tested, so it cannot have been motivated by the drug results
options.misconception: gets the direction of the historical relation backwards, since the drug results are what the account was built to explain

options.text: That some people improve without any drug, which contradicts the claim that the system is involved
options.misconception: treats spontaneous improvement as refuting a claim about involvement, when improvement can occur in both treated and untreated groups

questions.explanation: The asymmetry the objection names is real and it is the standard one. A treatment that acts on a system shows that the system is involved in the expression of symptoms; it does not show that the system produced the condition, because anything downstream of the cause would produce the same result. That is what the correct option states, and it is why accounts of this kind are described as accounts of the final common pathway rather than of a cause. The simplicity objection is not a scientific argument, since a parsimonious account is usually an advantage. The historical option reverses the relation, since the drug results are what such an account is ordinarily built to accommodate. The final option misreads the claim: involvement is not the claim that the drug is necessary, and improvement in untreated cases occurs in every treatment study of this kind, which is exactly why a comparison group exists.
questions.hint: Ask what a treatment that acts on a system can demonstrate about whether that system is where the condition begins.

questions.learningObjective: explain what a familial pattern does and does not license

options.misconception: equates a family pattern with a single-gene or highly heritable mechanism, which needs further evidence

options.text: That inherited factors are likely to contribute, while shared environment and non-shared environment remain live and the finding does not separate them
That relatives who share the condition do so because of the environment they share, since shared environment must be the operative factor
options.misconception: dismisses inheritance in favour of shared environment without any basis for excluding it

options.text: That the rate among relatives is high enough that exposure within the family is established as the route
options.misconception: calls an elevated rate a demonstrated route without any evidence of exposure

That the condition is more common in relatives is consistent with all three, which is why the careful conclusion is that inherited factors are likely to contribute rather than that they have been shown to be the cause. The analogy with height carries more than a family pattern licenses, since the resemblance hides the fact that separating inherited from shared contributions needs a design the family comparison does not provide. The third option simply asserts shared environment and rules inheritance out, which is the same error in the opposite direction. The final option treats an elevated rate among relatives as a demonstration of exposure, which would require evidence about what relatives were exposed to and an estimate of what that exposure does.
questions.hint: List everything besides inheritance that relatives share, and ask whether the finding separates them.

options.misconception: assumes only intensity changed, when the features named in the two periods are opposite in kind

options.text: A single episode of one kind that has become more severe, since a fall in energy followed by a rise in energy is a change of intensity
options.misconception: reduces a change from depression to elevated mood to a change of intensity within one episode

options.text: Two episodes of opposite polarity with no symptom-free interval between them, which is what the presence of features throughout is being used to decide

options.misconception: treats continuity of symptoms as evidence for two unrelated conditions rather than for a switch

options.misconception: overreads a negative medical investigation as though it had established a psychological cause

questions.learningObjective: state what a body-weight based criterion does and does not capture
questions.stem: One diagnosis in the eating-disorders group is defined in part by body weight being below a specified proportion of what is expected, and this criterion is required for the diagnosis. Which criticism is most substantial?

options.text: That weight cannot be measured accurately, since scales differ between clinics
options.misconception: raises a measurement-precision objection that standardising the measurement and recording the expected weight would address

options.text: That a weight criterion is late relative to other features, since restriction and other signs typically appear before the weight threshold is reached
That a weight criterion would exclude people who need care, since only people who are already very low can qualify
options.misconception: confuses a clinical need for care with eligibility for a specific diagnosis, which are different things

options.misconception: objects to precision on a factor that careful measurement controls, and ignores that the criterion has a defined threshold rather than a precise one

That is a real cost of the criterion and it is why a clinician who waits for the weight to be low enough may be acting after the point at which intervention is most useful. Scales can be standardised and the expected weight can be computed from a reference, so measurement inaccuracy is an avoidable procedural problem. Confusion of eligibility with clinical need misfires in the opposite direction, since the diagnosis is not a gate to care. And variation from fluid balance is a reason to measure carefully, not a reason to abandon a threshold.

questions.topic: Disorders: A Category Organised Around Identity
questions.learningObjective: explain what it means for a category to be defined by a disturbance of identity
questions.stem: A group of diagnoses are described as being defined chiefly by a disturbance in the sense of self, so that the problem is not a particular symptom but a pattern of how the person thinks, feels and behaves across situations. What does that organisation imply?

options.misconception: denies the possibility of assessment because the referent is a construct, without engaging with how such patterns are assessed

options.text: That these conditions are caused by a disturbance of identity rather than the other way round, which the definition settles
options.misconception: reads a descriptive definition as though it were a causal claim in a specific direction

options.text: That the classification is organising around a trait-like pattern, so a person may meet criteria in one context and not another while still having the same condition

The severity option asserts an ordering that the organising principle does not imply, since impairment depends on the person and the context.

questions.stem: One diagnosis in the personality-disorders group requires a pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others, and one of the listed features is a lack of remorse after doing harm. Which criticism is hardest to answer?

options.text: That the criterion is too vague to apply consistently, since disregard is not a measurable quantity
options.misconception: attacks vagueness in the abstract without addressing whether the criterion has been operationalised for assessment

options.text: That requiring evidence of harm is too demanding, since most people disregard others in small ways daily
options.misconception: substitutes ordinary everyday selfishness for a pattern, and calls a high bar a defect

options.text: That the criterion could be applied to any condition, since feeling no remorse is common in most disorders
options.misconception: invents a general base rate for absence of remorse that no evidence supports

options.text: That a lack of remorse reported by the person is unreliable evidence, since people do not have reliable access to it and can perform it convincingly

questions.explanation: This is a case where a criticism is genuinely hard to answer, and the reason is worth being precise about. The criterion is about the absence of a feeling, and feelings are exactly what people are least well placed to report about themselves, both because a genuine absence feels like nothing to report and because a reported one can be performed. That is a real measurement problem affecting the criterion, and it is not resolved by restating it, which is why this criticism is harder to dismiss than the others. It can be mitigated by triangulating against the behaviour and its consequences rather than relying on self-report alone, but not eliminated. The option calling the criterion vague addresses wording rather than the assessment procedure, which is where vagueness would actually be a problem. The option objecting to the harm requirement mistakes a pattern for everyday selfishness. The final option asserts a general base rate for absence of remorse that nobody has measured.
questions.hint: Ask which feature of the evidence is least available to the person being assessed, and whether anything else bears on it.

options.misconception: invents a fixed number of required interviews, which no scheme specifies

options.misconception: concedes the diagnosis is arbitrary while the repeated assessments are precisely what removes that worry

questions.topic: Disorders: Functioning Recorded Separately From Symptoms
questions.learningObjective: explain what a functioning measure adds to a symptom count
questions.stem: A diagnostic system records functioning in work, relationships and daily tasks separately from the number of symptoms. A person has five symptoms and is fully able to work and maintain relationships. Which statement best justifies recording functioning separately?

options.text: Because functioning is more important than symptoms for deciding what to do next
options.misconception: asserts a priority ordering that the two measures do not establish between them

options.text: Because a functioning rating can substitute for a symptom count where the count is unreliable
options.misconception: proposes a replacement rather than a supplement, which is not how the two are used

options.text: Because symptom count and functioning dissociate, so a count alone would lose the difference between a person who is unwell and coping and one who is not
Because functioning is easier to observe than symptoms, so recording it reduces the information needed
options.misconception: conflates the ease of observing behaviour with the presence of a symptom

The replacement option misdescribes the arrangement, since the functioning rating adds information the count does not carry rather than covering for the count's weaknesses. The final option confuses observable behaviour with the presence of a symptom, and a person can be fully functional while meeting every symptom criterion.
questions.hint: Ask whether the symptom count can distinguish the two situations the vignette describes, and what is lost if it cannot.

questions.topic: Disorders: A Discrepancy Account of a Learning Disorder
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a discrepancy account against the evidence
questions.stem: An account holds that a specific learning disorder exists where achievement in one area falls significantly below what general ability predicts, and the diagnosis requires that discrepancy. Which objection is most substantial?

options.misconception: cites an exclusion, which is a real concern but is about scope rather than about whether the discrepancy criterion is measurable

options.text: That the diagnosis would then be unnecessary, since a child reading well below the expectation is plainly impaired however the case is classified
options.misconception: infers redundancy from the obviousness of the impairment, which is a different argument from whether the criterion is sound

options.text: That achievement tests measure familiarity with schooling rather than the skill in question, since all achievement data come from school
options.misconception: confuses the source of achievement measures with what they measure

options.text: That ability and achievement measures are imperfectly correlated with each other, so the predicted score is uncertain and the discrepancy is partly measurement error

The consequence is that the size of the discrepancy that should be required cannot be set by anything other than convention, and cases near the line will be assigned inconsistently. That is the correct option, and it is an objection to the criterion rather than to the usefulness of the concept. The exclusion option raises a genuine scope concern about people with low average ability, and that is worth raising, but it is not an argument that the criterion cannot be computed. The redundancy option is a claim about clinical obviousness, which says nothing about whether the criterion is sound. The last option attacks the measures by their provenance rather than by what they assess, since measures are routinely used without anyone claiming they measure only familiarity.
questions.hint: Ask what quantity the discrepancy is defined as, and how precisely both of its terms can be known.

questions.learningObjective: explain why one term can come to denote two distinct conditions
questions.stem: One term has been applied both to a pattern of restricted and repetitive interests with early difficulties in social communication, and to a condition defined by an intolerance of change and inflexibility. Which statement best describes the situation?

That one of the two conditions has been wrongly named, so the older usage is the correct one and the newer is an error
options.misconception: supposes a naming disagreement is resolved by seniority, which is not how nomenclature is decided

options.text: That the two conditions are the same disorder seen at different ages, since restrictive interests occur before inflexibility does
options.misconception: converts a terminological overlap into a developmental sequence

options.text: That neither term can be used until the distinction is resolved, since clinical language cannot tolerate ambiguity
options.misconception: demands an absolute standard of terminology that no clinical vocabulary meets

Any statement of the form 'one in a hundred' becomes uninterpretable without knowing which definition was applied and to whom. That is what the correct option says. The seniority option mistakes a naming convention for a truth, and nothing about a term's age makes it more accurate. The developmental-sequence option turns a lexical overlap into an empirical claim about the order of features, which is a separate question with separate evidence. The final option sets a standard of terminology that clinical vocabularies have never met, and the practical response to an overlap is to say which definition was used rather than to stop using the word.

questions.topic: Disorders: Impairment Required in More Than One Setting
questions.learningObjective: explain the function of a multi-setting requirement

options.misconception: grounds a clinical criterion in staffing convenience

options.text: That features appearing in only one setting may be a response to that setting rather than a general condition, so two settings are evidence of generality
That impairment is easier to measure in a classroom than it is at home, so requiring two settings improves measurement
options.misconception: gives a reason for requiring two settings rather than the one where measurement is easiest

options.misconception: denies severity on the basis of narrowness, which is a non sequitur

Requiring them in two settings that differ in most respects is evidence that they belong to the person rather than to the place. The measurement option argues for requiring the easier setting, which is the opposite of what is required. The final option infers that a condition cannot be serious because it is narrow, which simply does not follow: something serious can be confined, and the point of the criterion is to avoid concluding from narrowness that nothing is wrong.

questions.topic: Disorders: Which Features Make a Substance-Use Diagnosis
questions.learningObjective: identify the criteria that distinguish a substance-use disorder from use
questions.stem: Three statements about the criteria for a substance-use diagnosis are offered. Two are supported and one is not. Select the two supported statements.

options.text: Impaired control over use, such as taking more than intended or being unable to cut down, is one of the criteria
Using the substance to cope with a negative mood that began before the substance was used is one of the criteria
options.misconception: lists a common accompanying behaviour as a diagnostic criterion, when the criteria turn on control and consequences rather than on why the substance is used

options.text: Continued use despite harm to health or to work that the person acknowledges is connected to the use is one of the criteria
That the substance must have been taken daily for a fixed period before the diagnosis can be considered
options.misconception: invents a frequency and duration requirement that the criteria do not contain

questions.topic: Disorders: Use That Is Not a Disorder
questions.learningObjective: explain why use alone does not meet a disorder diagnosis
questions.stem: A person drinks wine most evenings, around two glasses, has no health problems, has not been unable to stop, and gets no pleasure from stopping. On the criteria described in the previous item, what follows?

options.text: That the pattern is a disorder, since drinking most evenings is frequent use and frequency is a criterion
options.misconception: treats frequency as a criterion, which is exactly what the correct option denies

options.text: That the pattern cannot be assessed without a clinical interview, since the criteria depend on information not given here
options.misconception: insists on a data source the vignette already supplies, since the criteria are all present in the description

options.text: That the pattern is necessarily healthy, since no disorder is present and absence of disorder implies health
options.misconception: infers health from absence of diagnosis, which is a different claim

options.text: That frequency and quantity are not the criteria, so this pattern does not meet them unless control or consequences show a problem

Drinking most evenings is frequent and the amount is not trivial, and neither fact is among the criteria. What the criteria ask about is whether control has been impaired and whether use continues despite consequences, and the description gives no health problem, no inability to stop, and no acknowledged harm. So on the information given the pattern does not meet the criteria. That is the correct answer, and the careful part is the qualification in it: a description this brief could certainly be concealing a problem, which is why a clinician would ask rather than conclude, and why the item says unless rather than asserting flatly that no disorder is present. The final option is a general logical error: absence of a diagnosis is not a finding of health, and plenty of conditions go undiagnosed.
questions.hint: Check each criterion against the description, and notice that none of them is about how often or how much.

questions.topic: Disorders: Return to Use After a Period Without It
questions.learningObjective: explain why return to use is treated as a feature of a course rather than a failure of will
questions.stem: A substantial proportion of people treated for a substance-use disorder return to use at some point. Which treatment of that fact is most defensible?

options.text: Treat it as information about the condition and about the treatment, so it points at what needs to change rather than at the person's character
Treat it as evidence that the treatment does not work, since an effective treatment would prevent any return to use
options.misconception: sets an absolute standard, when the relevant question is the rate relative to what happens without treatment

options.text: Treat it as evidence that the person did not really want to stop, since the behaviour is inconsistent with the stated goal
options.misconception: infers sincerity from behaviour, ignoring that wanting to stop and being able to stop are different things

options.text: Treat it as a normal part of the course of any long-term condition, so it should not be reported at all
options.misconception: normalises the rate to the point of removing the information, and rates differ markedly by condition and treatment

questions.explanation: How return to use is interpreted depends entirely on what it is being treated as evidence about. If it is evidence about the person, it becomes a character judgement, and that framing makes the information useless because it generates no next step. If it is evidence about the condition and the treatment, it becomes the most useful datum available, because it tells a clinician which components to strengthen, which is the whole reason for tracking it. That reframing is the correct option and it is the difference between an approach that can improve outcomes and one that cannot. The option declaring the treatment ineffective sets an absolute standard where the relevant comparison is against the rate without treatment, and by that standard treatments do reduce it. The sincerity option confuses wanting and being able, and every clinical approach in this area treats the gap between them as the target. The final option overcorrects into suppressing information that varies by condition and treatment and is worth reporting.
questions.hint: Ask what action each interpretation leads to, since an interpretation that produces no next step is not useful.

questions.learningObjective: explain what a symptom score omits and why a second measure is added

options.misconception: understates what a symptom score omits, since the score never measured bothersomeness at all

options.text: That their level of functioning at work and at home had not changed at all over the same period
That the score fell by the same amount in a comparison group that received no treatment
options.misconception: refutes a causal claim rather than showing what the score omits, and the item asks about the score's coverage

options.text: That a second measure taken at the same time gave the same result, since agreement between measures would rule out a real change
options.misconception: inverts the role of convergent evidence, which strengthens rather than undermines a finding

A halving of the score alongside no change at all in functioning is therefore evidence that the score moved without the person's situation changing, which directly weakens the claim that the treatment helped them. The comparison-group option is about whether the change was caused by the treatment, which is a different question from what the score captures, and is addressed by the design rather than by the choice of measure. The final option treats agreement between measures as disconfirmation, when two measures agreeing is exactly what one hopes to see.
questions.hint: Ask what the score is built from, and therefore what it cannot register.

questions.topic: Treatment: A Therapist Cannot Be Blind to the Treatment Being Delivered
questions.learningObjective: explain what blinding can and cannot accomplish in a treatment trial
questions.stem: In a trial of a talking therapy, the participants are told which condition they are in so that expectations can be measured. Which statement about blinding in this setting is correct?

options.text: That neither can be blinded, since a talking therapy necessarily reveals itself through what the therapist says and does
options.misconception: overstates the impossibility, since participants' expectations about the therapy's contents are what can be concealed

options.text: That blinding the participants would be unethical, since a person must always know what treatment they are receiving
options.misconception: invents an ethical requirement, where the relevant considerations are consent and how the allocation is explained

options.text: That participants can often be blinded while the therapist cannot, so the design can address expectation while leaving the therapist's contribution unaddressed
That the therapist's expectations can be blinded by not telling the therapist which hypothesis is being tested
options.misconception: confuses concealing the hypothesis with blinding the therapist, who remains the one delivering the treatment

questions.explanation: The two roles can be blinded quite differently and it is worth separating them. A participant's expectation about what a therapy contains can be concealed well enough to compare conditions on that expectation, which is a real and common source of influence in this literature. A therapist delivering the treatment necessarily knows what it is, and no arrangement removes that knowledge. So the design can address the participant side and leaves the therapist side open, and a good report says so rather than claiming the trial was double-blind. That is the correct option. The option declaring both impossible confuses the contents of a therapy, which participants are not told in detail, with the fact that a therapy is being delivered. The option inventing an ethical prohibition confuses consent, which is about agreeing to a procedure, with knowledge of a hypothesis. The final option mistakes concealing the study's hypothesis from the investigator for blinding, and even then it is the participant who forms the expectation.
questions.hint: Ask who needs to know what in order for their expectations to be shaped, and whether that is the same for both roles.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Treatment: The Share of Improvement Not Accounted for by the Comparison Group
questions.learningObjective: compute the share of observed improvement exceeding the comparison-group rate
questions.stem: In a trial, 80 people receive the treatment and 41 of them improve. In a comparison group of 80 who receive nothing, 12 improve. The comparison group's improvement rate is therefore 0.15. Taking that rate as the improvement expected without the treatment, what share of the treatment group's improvers is not accounted for by it?
questions.explanation: The comparison group's rate is 12 out of 80, which is 0.15, and applying that rate to the treatment group of the same size gives an expectation of 12 improvers there. The treatment group actually had 41, so the excess over what the comparison rate accounts for is 41 minus 12, which is 29. As a share of the treatment group's improvers, 29 over 41 is 0.707, so 0.71. The reason the item is worth doing carefully rather than quickly is that three figures are in play and each has its own role. The rate difference is 51 percent against 15 percent, which is 36 percentage points, and that is the more interpretable measure of the benefit because it is on the same scale as the outcome. The ratio is 3.4. The share computed here is a proportion of the observed improvers, so it answers a narrower question: of the people who improved, what fraction did so by more than the comparison rate would predict. That is not a standard effect measure and it should not be read as one, since it depends on the response rate as well as on the comparison, and a treatment with a lower response rate can produce a higher value of it. The reason the quantity matters at all is that a report of 41 out of 80 counts improvement that would be expected without the treatment, and any figure that includes the expected share should say so.
questions.hint: Apply the comparison rate to the treatment group's size, subtract that expectation from the 41 who improved, and divide by 41.

questions.topic: Treatment: Withdrawals Counted Against the Group That Started
questions.learningObjective: compute completion rates with the correct denominator for each arm
questions.stem: A trial randomises 240 people, 120 to the treatment and 120 to the comparison. Thirty in the treatment arm and twenty in the comparison arm withdraw before the end. What share of the whole randomised cohort remained to the end, to two decimal places as a proportion?
questions.explanation: Fifty people withdrew in total, since thirty plus twenty is fifty, and 240 minus 50 is 190, so 190 over 240 is 0.7917, which is 0.79 to two decimal places. The denominators are the point of this item rather than the division. The treatment arm kept 90 of its 120, which is 0.75, and the comparison arm kept 100 of its 120, which is 0.833, so completion differs between the arms by 8.3 percentage points. That difference matters more than the overall figure, because the arms are no longer the same people: if withdrawal is related to how well someone is doing, which it usually is, then the remaining treatment group and the remaining comparison group are not comparable even though they started as one. The overall share also invites a specific error, since one quarter of 240 would be 60 and only 50 withdrew, so a report saying that a quarter withdrew would be wrong by five people, and the error would be invisible in the conclusion. The figure to report is therefore all three: the completion rate in each arm separately and the total number who contributed data.
questions.hint: Subtract each arm's withdrawals from that arm's own size, and treat the difference between the arms as part of the answer.

options.misconception: draws a causal conclusion from a change over time with nothing to rule out other causes of it

On many conditions it is not small. So the design gives a description and cannot give an attribution. The causal option makes the inference the design exists to prevent. The universal-response option sets a standard that no treatment in any field meets, including those with no serious alternatives. The final option is too strong: uncontrolled series are a legitimate design, useful for description, for feasibility and for generating hypotheses, and they are simply unable to support an attribution.

The options each use a count that is present in the table but is not one of the two rates. The second uses the non-improvement counts, which reverses the direction, since more not improving in the comparison group means a bigger benefit in the treatment group rather than a smaller one. The third never subtracts. The fourth mixes one group's non-improvement count into a ratio.

questions.topic: Treatment: What the Weighting in a Combined Figure Assumes
questions.learningObjective: interpret what a sample-size weighted average of effects does to a small study
questions.stem: Two studies of the same treatment report an effect of 0.20 from 40 participants and an effect of 0.50 from 160 participants. Combining them with a weight proportional to the number of participants, what is the combined effect to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: The weighted average is the sum of each effect times its weight, over the sum of the weights, and with weights of 40 and 160 that is 40 times 0.20 plus 160 times 0.50, which is 8 plus 80, or 88, divided by 200, giving 0.44. The number is not difficult and the interpretation is the content of the item. Weighting by sample size means the larger study dominates, and here four fifths of the weight sits on the study reporting 0.50. An unweighted average of the two would be 0.35, so the choice of weighting moves the headline figure by nearly 0.09, which is larger than the difference most treatments are trying to demonstrate. A reader who saw only 0.44 would have no way of knowing that a defensible alternative weighting gives 0.35, so a combined figure is only interpretable alongside the weights used and the spread of the underlying estimates. There is also a second assumption buried in the calculation, which is that the two studies estimate the same quantity; if they differ in population, in outcome measure or in how long they followed people up, then averaging them produces a figure that describes neither, however carefully the arithmetic is done.
questions.hint: Multiply each effect by its sample size, add, and divide by the total sample size. Then check how far the unweighted average sits from it.

questions.topic: Treatment: How Much of a Gain Is Still There at Follow-Up
questions.learningObjective: compute the share of an initial gain retained at follow-up
questions.stem: A group of patients scores 20 on a symptom measure before treatment, 8 at the end of treatment, and 12 at a follow-up three months later. As a proportion, how much of the gain achieved during treatment was still present at follow-up?
