The share retained is therefore 8 over 12, which is 0.667, so 0.67. The reason this quantity is worth computing separately from the follow-up score is that a follow-up score and a retained gain answer different questions. Someone reading the score of 12 alone has to reconstruct the whole trajectory, and a score of 12 looks like a partial return to baseline without the reader noticing that two thirds of what was achieved is still there. Conversely, a treatment that produced a larger initial gain and kept less of it could end at the same follow-up score while being the worse treatment, which is why the pair of figures is needed. One caveat belongs with any such computation: a comparison group is required to say whether the retained gain is attributable to the treatment, since some of the loss over three months would be expected without it, and the report as described gives no comparison group.
questions.hint: Compute the gain at each time point from the baseline, then divide the retained gain by the initial gain.

questions.topic: Treatment: An Effect Size With and Without the Small-Sample Correction
questions.learningObjective: read a treatment effect with an interval and a bias-corrected effect size
questions.stem: A trial compares 60 treated with 60 comparison patients. Mean scores are 14.2 and 17.8, with standard deviations of 9.0 and 9.4, on a scale where lower is better. The pooled standard deviation is 9.20, and 118 degrees of freedom apply. Which set of figures is right?

options.text: A difference of 3.6 points, an effect size of 0.49, a 95 percent interval on the difference from 0.27 to 6.93, and p of about .03
options.misconception: divides the difference by one group's standard deviation rather than by the pooled one, which inflates the effect size

options.text: A difference of 3.6 points, an effect size of 0.39, a 95 percent interval on the difference from 0.27 to 6.93, and p of about .03
A difference of 3.6 points, an effect size of 0.39, a 95 percent interval on the difference from 0.27 to 6.93, and p of about .50
options.misconception: halves the two-sided p value instead of doubling the smaller tail, so it reports half the correct value

options.text: A difference of 3.6 points, an effect size of 0.39, a 95 percent interval on the difference from 0.30 to 6.90, and p of about .03
options.misconception: quotes an interval that does not match the standard error of the difference, so the endpoints are inconsistent with the other figures

questions.explanation: Each figure has to come out of the arithmetic and they are consistent. The difference is 17.8 minus 14.2, which is 3.6 points in the direction favouring treatment, since lower is better. The effect size is 3.6 over 9.20, which is 0.391, so 0.39. The standard error of the difference is the pooled standard deviation times the square root of one over 60 plus one over 60, which is 1.680. With 118 degrees of freedom the critical value is 1.980, so the interval runs from 3.6 minus 1.980 times 1.680, which is 0.27, to 6.93. The t statistic is 3.6 over 1.680, which is 2.14, and a two-sided p on 118 degrees of freedom at that t is about 0.034. That is the correct set and the reasoning is what makes it checkable. questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Treatment: A Community Prevalence Figure and an Interval Around It
questions.learningObjective: compute an interval for a proportion and compare it with a naive one
questions.stem: A community survey of 600 people records 47 who meet criteria for a disorder, which is 7.83 percent. Using the interval method that behaves well at proportions away from one half, what is the upper end of the 95 percent interval on that share, as a percentage?
questions.explanation: The method behaves well at moderate proportions is the Wilson score interval, and it is used here because the naive interval built from the square-root-of-p-times-one-minus-p-over-n formula is badly wrong at this share. The Wilson interval with 47 successes out of 600 gives bounds of 5.94 percent and 10.26 percent, so the upper end is 10.26 and that is the keyed value. The reason the naive interval fails is specific and worth knowing, because it is the interval most often reported by default. The naive bounds run from 5.68 to 9.98 percent, which are both too narrow, and the reason is that the standard error it uses treats the sample proportion as though it were known rather than estimated. With 47 events the count is small enough that the normal approximation behind it is poor, and the interval ends up understating the uncertainty by a visible margin. The practical consequence is that two surveys with overlapping Wilson intervals but non-overlapping naive intervals can be wrongly reported as differing. Any answer should say which method produced it, because the two methods give different numbers from the same 47 out of 600 and a reader cannot otherwise tell which rule was followed.
questions.hint: Use the score interval, which is the one that stays well behaved away from one half, and compute its upper bound as a percentage.

questions.topic: Treatment: How Many Participants a Trial of a Given Size Can Detect
questions.learningObjective: interpret a power figure and the sample size it implies
questions.stem: A trial with 40 participants in each group and a two-sided alpha of .05 has a power of 0.60 against an effect size of 0.5, and a power of 0.94 against an effect size of 0.8. A second trial needs 64 per group to reach 80 percent power against an effect size of 0.5. Which statement about these figures is correct?

options.text: That the first trial is adequately powered because it has 80 participants in total, since the total is what determines power
options.misconception: asserts a sufficient total without comparing it to anything, which supplies no basis for calling it adequate

options.text: That the second trial is overpowered, since needing more participants for a smaller effect must be a mistake
options.misconception: inverts the relationship, since needing more participants for a smaller effect is exactly what the arithmetic requires

options.text: That power does not depend on the effect size, since the sample size and the alpha level fix it entirely
options.misconception: drops one of the three quantities that determine power, which makes the 0.60 and 0.86 figures impossible

options.text: That the first trial could miss a real effect of 0.5 about two times in five, so a null result there would be uninformative

questions.explanation: The reading of the first figure is the one that matters clinically. A power of 0.60 against an effect of 0.5 means that if a real effect of that size existed, this trial would fail to detect it about four times in ten, and four times in ten is the probability of a false negative. So a null result from this trial is uninformative: it is substantially more likely under the no-effect condition than an adequately powered null would be, and the correct conclusion is that the trial could not have found the effect, not that there was none. That is the correct option and it is the single most consequential thing to understand about small trials. The second figure in the stem is included to show that the same trial is well able to detect a larger effect, which matters because it locates the problem precisely: the inadequacy is not that 40 per group is too few for anything, it is that 40 per group is too few for an effect of 0.5 specifically, and power rises steeply with effect size. That is also why the third figure is larger than the trial already has: detecting half a standard deviation needs 64 per group where detecting four fifths of one needs 40. The second option has no comparison to offer and so cannot settle adequacy. The third reverses the relationship, since a smaller effect is harder to detect and requires more participants, which is arithmetic rather than error. The final option omits the effect size from the three quantities that determine power, which is why the two power figures in the stem differ at all.
questions.hint: Ask what a power of 0.60 implies about how often a real effect would be missed, and what a null result from such a trial means.

options.text: That the group should have been split before the trial, since outcomes could not be mixed within a diagnosis

questions.topic: Treatment: What Four Statements About These Designs Claim
questions.learningObjective: judge which statements about treatment trials are supported

A trial with a comparison group can show that the treatment caused the difference, because random allocation removes every other influence
options.misconception: credits random allocation with removing influences it does not touch, such as anything the participants bring to the study

options.text: A trial can report that the difference it found was unlikely to have arisen by chance, given the assumptions of the test used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Treatment: What the Trial Designs Leave Open
questions.learningObjective: state the limits of the trial evidence for making treatment decisions
questions.stem: Randomised controlled trials are the standard evidence for whether a treatment works. Explain what that evidence still leaves unresolved for someone deciding what to offer a particular patient.

answer.exemplar: The trial answer and the clinical question are not the same question, and the gap between them is worth spelling out rather than treating the trial as though it settled the decision. A trial can establish, under its own assumptions, that two groups differed and by how much. Several things sit outside that. Effect sizes are averages, and heterogeneity within a diagnosis is the norm rather than the exception, so a mean of 0.4 is consistent with a distribution in which a substantial minority do not respond at all, and a reader planning treatment for one person needs something the mean cannot supply. The population in a trial is selected, and selection is not random with respect to the thing being studied: severity, comorbidity, previous attempts, motivation and concurrent treatment all vary systematically between participants and the people a clinician actually sees, so the average effect in the trial need not be the expected effect for a given patient. Trials are also underpowered for harms, because the sample size is set by what is needed to detect an intended benefit, so a trial showing a common benefit can say almost nothing about a rare side effect. Follow-up is usually short relative to the timescale on which gains erode or side effects accumulate, and a result measured two weeks after treatment ends is not a result about a year of treatment. Comparison groups are rarely inert, and a comparison that involves attention but no specific treatment produces an estimate against that comparator rather than against nothing. Then there is the question of what counts as a meaningful change, which the trial's statistical machinery does not address: a difference can be reliable and too small for a patient to notice, and the answer to that requires a comparison with a within-patient improvement rather than between patients. Finally, trials establish effects on average and are largely silent on mechanisms, so they rarely tell a clinician what to do when a patient does not respond, since the next treatment would then be chosen on a rationale the evidence has not supplied. What would narrow the gap: individual participant data analyses to see who benefits and why, trials that recruit closer to clinic populations, pre-specified harms monitoring with samples adequate to detect them, follow-up durations matched to the timescale of the outcome, and reporting of responder analyses alongside means with their own denominators.

questions.explanation: The answer has to name the specific gaps rather than gesturing at generalisability: heterogeneity hidden by a mean, the non-random selection of trial participants, trials being powered for benefit and not for harms, short follow-up relative to the timescale of change, non-inert comparators, the absence of any account of what meaningfulness is, and silence on mechanisms and on what to do for non-responders. It should propose the analyses and design choices that would narrow each gap.
questions.hint: Ask what a trial measures on average, what it selects for, how long it looks, and what it never examines.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Disorders and Treatment: What a Mean Hides Beside What a Diagnosis Hides
questions.learningObjective: synthesise the parallel between heterogeneity within a diagnosis and within an outcome
questions.stem: A diagnosis is described as a category with cases that differ from one another, and a treatment trial reports that the mean improvement for the diagnosed group was 4 points with a standard deviation of 6. Synthesise what these two facts jointly imply for deciding what to offer one person.

answer.exemplar: The two facts are parallel in structure, and seeing them as parallel is what makes either one tractable, because each says the same thing at a different level: the quantity being used to group or summarise people is not homogeneous inside itself. A diagnosis groups together people who meet a shared set of criteria, and those criteria were chosen to be reliable rather than homogeneous, so two people carrying the same label may differ in mechanism, in severity, in what precipitated it and in what maintains it. A mean improvement does the same thing to outcomes, summarising a distribution in which a substantial fraction responded substantially and another fraction did not respond at all. The consequence for a decision about one person is the same in both cases and it is a limitation of the summary rather than a defect of it: neither the label nor the mean tells you what to expect for a particular individual, and anyone who reports a treatment effect of 4 points and implies that a given patient should expect 4 points has made an inference the statistic does not support. Two further features of the parallel are worth stating. The heterogeneity within a diagnosis and the heterogeneity within an outcome are not independent, since a category whose cases share a mechanism would be expected to respond more alike than one whose cases do not, and so responder analyses can in principle bear on whether a category should be subdivided at all. And the overlap is a reason to prefer responder analyses to means for decision-making while recognising that they carry their own problems, since a responder analysis has to define a responder, and the definition chosen can change the answer. What would actually help is a combination: the diagnosis reported alongside the heterogeneity within it, so that a clinician knows the label's spread, and the outcome reported as a distribution with responder proportions and denominators stated, so that a clinician can see whether the patient in front of them resembles the group that benefited. Reporting only the mean, or only the diagnosis, conceals the same thing in each case.

questions.explanation: The answer has to state that the two facts share a structure, explain what that structure costs for an individual decision, note that the two heterogeneities are not independent and that responder analyses can bear on both, and close with what should be reported alongside each summary. It should acknowledge that a responder analysis needs its own definition rather than presenting it as a free solution.
questions.hint: Ask what the label and the mean have in common, and what each conceals about the people inside it.

questions.learningObjective: evaluate the claim that combining treatments is necessarily better

If the combination is no better than the better component alone, then the second treatment contributed nothing detectable, and since it carries its own cost, its own appointments and its own side effects, the combination is not worth taking. That is what the correct option says and it is the pattern a well-run trial of a combination frequently finds. The second option states the opposite pattern, which is the one that supports the combination. The third asserts a general relation between the number of treatments and harm that does not hold, and a combination outperforming neither is also not the pattern being asked about. The final option is subtler and worth handling carefully: one component beating the combination is consistent with the added component being inert, since if it were harmful in combination one would expect the combination to fall below both, so this pattern still fails to establish interference.
questions.hint: Ask what the combination has to beat for the second treatment to be worth adding, and which pattern fails to clear that bar.
